query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. In that context, which method can be used for investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, and why?

generation.hypothesis: When heated in an in situ aberration‐corrected TEM with a heating stage, nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will display only minimal atomic-scale structural changes, supporting the idea that enhanced thermal stability arises from thermodynamic contributions.
generation.material_initial_state: Nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles with a high-entropy alloy configuration showing a uniform lattice structure at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Heating the nanoparticles within an aberration‐corrected TEM using an integrated heating stage.
generation.conditions: A high-temperature, vacuum environment inside the TEM, with temperatures ramped gradually to the target range without exceeding the melting or sintering threshold.
generation.structural_mediator: Subtle atomic rearrangements, minimal defect formation, or very slight diffusional changes visible in high-resolution TEM images and diffraction patterns.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of the nearly equiatomic multi‐metal nanoparticles reduces the driving force for phase transitions and atomic diffusion at elevated temperatures, thereby maintaining structural integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nanoparticles will show limited atomic-scale rearrangement or phase change under high-temperature conditions, in contrast to nanoparticles with lower configurational entropy which might exhibit more pronounced structural changes.
generation.baseline: Atomic structure and lattice parameters observed at room temperature prior to heating.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies only up to temperatures that do not induce complete nanoparticle melting, sintering, or other irreversible morphological changes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the minimal atomic changes is uncertain, and subtle transient phases or very short-lived rearrangements may occur below the resolution limit of the TEM.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ aberration‐corrected TEM experiments with a controlled heating stage on AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, capturing atomic-scale images and diffraction patterns at incrementally increased temperatures up to the pre-determined limit.
measurements: High-resolution TEM images documenting atomic positions and lattice periodicity
Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns to monitor changes in crystal structure
Temperature calibration readings from the heating stage
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the TEM data reveal significant atomic rearrangements, phase transformations, or defect aggregations at temperatures below the expected thermal threshold (indicating a loss of structural integrity) rather than only very minor changes, then the hypothesis that the enhanced thermal stability is due to thermodynamic contributions is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization

Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
